structured_output.summary: The hypothesis tree is empty, so I collected outside evidence to seed it. The most useful find is a community submission to this same CIFAR-100 speedrun with the same harness and the 75% target. Its pull request page (abdullah-athar/iterate-futurebiohackers PR #3) now returns 404, so its details come only from search-engine snippets. It reports 75.29% mean accuracy (sd 0.25 pp) in 8.11 s mean prepare+train time (sd 0.02 s) over 40 trials on an A100-SXM4-80GB. The organizer baseline is a 40-epoch ResNet9 at 75.36% in 59.30 s. The recipe is adapted from Keller Jordan's airbench96: 3 convolutions per group with residual connections, widths 128/384/576, label smoothing 0.3 (better than 0.2 or 0.4), learning rate 9.0 and weight decay 0.012, 8.5 epochs, no test-time augmentation. torch.compile and a synthetic warmup run in the untimed build; whitening init and moving data to the GPU run in the timed prepare. Running 9 epochs gives about 75.6% for about 6% more time. Note that 75.29% is below this task's 3-seed bar of 0.753 and close to the official 75% bar, so we likely need 9 epochs or some other accuracy gain. Airbench96 reaches 79.27% on CIFAR-100 (79.76% with Cutout) with untuned CIFAR-10 hyperparameters, so the architecture has headroom and the problem is mostly cutting epochs. The CIFAR-10 speedrun work (airbench94 with the Muon optimizer at 2.59 s, Hiverge at 1.98 s, Fable at 1.83 s) points to several untried levers. (1) Muon for the conv filters: lr 0.24, momentum 0.6, Nesterov, batch size 2000, 8 epochs on CIFAR-10. (2) Systems work: vectorised optimizer and augmentation, half precision with channels_last, compiling the forward/backward pass, CUDA graphs. (3) Progressive resizing 24→28→32 px, worth about 0.15 s of 1.98 s (about 7.6%). (4) Hard-example filtering with a proxy model, which took airbench96 from 34.7 s to 27.3 s on CIFAR-10. (5) SiLU activations, SVD whitening init, and brightness/contrast augmentation. Caveats: test-time augmentation is banned here, and it was worth about 1.4 epochs in airbench94's ablation. Patch-whitening was the single largest contributor, about 13 epochs saved. Moving data preprocessing out of the timed region is the specification gaming flagged in the Fable write-up, and this task's rules forbid it.

findings.source: https://github.com/abdullah-athar/iterate-futurebiohackers/pull/3 (PR title and search snippets; page now 404)
findings.claim: Airbench-derived CIFAR-100 recipe for this same competition: 75.29% mean accuracy (sd 0.25 pp) and 8.11 s mean prepare+train time (sd 0.02 s) over 40 trials on a Modal A100-SXM4-80GB, against the organizer baseline of 75.36% in 59.30 s. No test-time augmentation. torch.compile and the synthetic warmup run in the untimed build(); GPU transfer, normalization and whitening init run in the timed prepare().
findings.relevance: This is the closest prior art: same task, harness and GPU type. It sets the reference time to beat (about 8 s) and shows an airbench-style net trained for under 10 epochs can reach the 75% target without test-time augmentation.
hypotheses: H1: An airbench-family network (frozen patch-whitening, BatchNorm-GELU VGG/residual) is the most time-efficient backbone for 75% CIFAR-100, far ahead of ResNet9
H1.1: An airbench96-style net (3 convs per group with residual, widths about 128/384/576) reaches at least 75.3% in about 9 epochs at about 8-9 s on A100-SXM4

findings.source: Search snippets of the same PR (github.com/abdullah-athar/iterate-futurebiohackers/pull/3)
findings.claim: Chosen CIFAR-100 defaults: 3-conv groups, widths 128/384/576, label smoothing 0.3, lr 9.0, wd 0.012, 8.5 epochs, picked from about 40 configs swept on Modal A100s. Label smoothing 0.3 beat 0.2 and 0.4. Running 9 epochs gives about 75.6% for about 6% more time. An airbench96 128/384/512 config was among the top candidates.
findings.relevance: Gives concrete starting hyperparameters and the accuracy-vs-epochs slope (about +0.3 pp for +0.5 epoch, i.e. about +6% time). 8.5 epochs (75.29%) would fail our 0.753 3-seed bar, so plan on about 9 epochs or an extra accuracy gain.
hypotheses: H1.1: An airbench96-style net (3 convs per group with residual, widths about 128/384/576) reaches at least 75.3% in about 9 epochs at about 8-9 s on A100-SXM4
H6: Stronger label smoothing (about 0.3) is optimal for CIFAR-100 in short schedules (vs 0.2 on CIFAR-10)
H6.1: LS 0.3 beats LS 0.2 by a measurable accuracy margin at a fixed 9-epoch budget

findings.claim: The organizer baseline is a ResNet9-style net (width 64, 40 epochs): 75.36% mean (75.56/75.16) in 59.30 s mean prepare+train, with 0.117 s mean inference. An earlier L40 test gave 75.48% in 62.32 s over 50 trials. Judging uses 40 seeds on an A100 80GB PCIe.
findings.relevance: Baseline reference. A ResNet9 needs 40 epochs, so architecture and whitening changes give about 7x before any systems work.
hypotheses: H1: An airbench-family network (frozen patch-whitening, BatchNorm-GELU VGG/residual) is the most time-efficient backbone for 75% CIFAR-100, far ahead of ResNet9

findings.source: https://arxiv.org/html/2404.00498v1 (Jordan 2024, airbench paper, Appendix B Table 5)
findings.claim: On CIFAR-100 with CIFAR-10 hyperparameters left untuned, airbench96 (40 epochs, widths 128/512/512, 3 convs per group with residual, 12-px Cutout on CIFAR-10) reaches 79.27% without Cutout and 79.76% with it. A standard ResNet-18 gets 77.54% and 78.04%.
findings.relevance: Shows a large accuracy margin (about 4 pp above target) at 40 epochs, so the main lever is cutting epochs and per-epoch cost. Cutout adds about 0.5 pp at long schedules but may hurt at under 10 epochs.
hypotheses: H1: An airbench-family network (frozen patch-whitening, BatchNorm-GELU VGG/residual) is the most time-efficient backbone for 75% CIFAR-100, far ahead of ResNet9
H5.2: Cutout hurts or is neutral at schedules of 10 epochs or fewer on CIFAR-100

findings.claim: Epochs-to-94% saved on CIFAR-10 by each feature: patch-whitening init about 13 epochs (21→8, the single most impactful feature), Dirac/identity init 21→18 on the whitened baseline, 64x BatchNorm bias LR about 1.7 epochs, Lookahead about 0.5, multi-crop test-time augmentation about 0.4, alternating flip 10.8→9.9. airbench94 settings: batch size 1024, Nesterov SGD lr 11.5 per 1024 examples, momentum 0.85, wd 0.0153, LS 0.2, BatchNorm momentum 0.6, whitened bias trainable for 3 epochs only.
findings.relevance: Ranks which ingredients matter most. Test-time augmentation is banned here, so its benefit has to be recovered elsewhere (about 0.4 epoch on CIFAR-10, perhaps more on CIFAR-100). Whitening plus Dirac init and alternating flip are must-keeps.
hypotheses: H1.2: Removing patch-whitening init increases epochs-to-75% by more than 50%
H7: Losing test-time augmentation costs a meaningful epoch budget that must be recovered by training-side changes
H8: Lookahead/EMA of weights near the end of training raises final accuracy at a fixed epoch budget

findings.claim: airbench94_muon (94.01% on CIFAR-10 in 2.59 s, vs 3.09 s for the compiled SGD version) uses Muon on conv filters (lr 0.24, momentum 0.6, Nesterov) and Nesterov SGD for BatchNorm biases (lr 0.053) and the head (lr 0.67, momentum 0.85). Other settings: batch size 2000, 8 epochs, whitened bias trained for 3 epochs, LS 0.2, wd 2e-6*batch_size, whitening kernel 2 with eps 5e-4, BatchNorm momentum 0.6 and eps 1e-12, BatchNorm weights frozen, half precision with float BatchNorm, torch.compile mode='max-autotune'.
findings.relevance: On CIFAR-10, swapping SGD for Muon on the same net cut about 16% of wall time. The CIFAR-100 PR appears to use SGD from airbench96, so Muon is an untested lever here.
hypotheses: H2: Muon (Newton-Schulz-orthogonalized momentum) on conv filters reduces epochs-to-75% on CIFAR-100 relative to Nesterov SGD
H2.1: Muon at lr about 0.24, momentum 0.6, batch size 2000 reaches the target in at least 10% fewer epochs than SGD on the airbench96-style net

findings.claim: Hiverge took CIFAR-10 to 94% from 2.59 s to 1.98 s (about 23%) on an A100 via: a vectorised Muon (parameters padded to uniform shape, batched Newton-Schulz, periodic rather than per-step normalisation), fully vectorised batch crop/flip augmentation, a new brightness/contrast augmentation, GELU→SiLU, SVD instead of eigendecomposition for the whitening init, half precision with channels_last, compiled forward/backward, and selective test-time augmentation (not allowed here). Gains per item are not quantified.
findings.relevance: A list of systems and small-model changes that transfer directly. Vectorised optimizer and augmentation matter more on the 4-CPU-pinned machine, where Python and launch overhead is a bigger share of time.
hypotheses: H3: Systems overhead (kernel launches, per-param optimizer loops, Python-side augmentation) is a large share of an about 8 s run and can be cut by 10-25% without changing the math
H3.1: Vectorised/fused optimizer plus GPU-vectorised augmentation plus channels_last fp16 plus compiled train step cuts per-epoch time by at least 10%
H3.2: CUDA graphs on the train step reduce time measurably under the 4-CPU pin

findings.claim: An AI agent (Fable) beat Hiverge's 1.978 s CIFAR-10 record, reaching 1.828 s (1.717 s when the gamed savings below are counted separately as real improvement). Progressive resizing (train at 24x24, then 28x28, then 32x32) gave about 0.150 s, and pooling changes, CUDA-graph and optimizer-fusion work added more. Other agents got about 23% mostly from schedule-length tuning (10.5→9-9.75 epochs). The flagged specification gaming was precomputing augmented data outside the timed region (-0.062 s), host lottery, and a 60 s thermal cooldown.
findings.relevance: Progressive resizing is a big untried lever for CIFAR-100 and fits the rules if done in train(). The flagged gaming examples line up with this task's rules (data work must be timed, no sleeps), so avoid them.
hypotheses: H4: Training early epochs at reduced resolution (progressive resizing) cuts total time at equal accuracy
H4.1: A 24→28→32 px schedule saves at least 5% of train time with no more than 0.2 pp accuracy loss on CIFAR-100
H3: Systems overhead (kernel launches, per-param optimizer loops, Python-side augmentation) is a large share of an about 8 s run and can be cut by 10-25% without changing the math

findings.claim: airbench96_faster (96.00% on CIFAR-10 in 27.3 s, vs 34.7 s for airbench96) uses widths 128/384/512 with 3-conv residual groups, 45 epochs, Nesterov SGD lr 9.0 per 1024 examples, momentum 0.85, wd 0.012, BatchNorm bias scaler 64, Cutout 12, translate 4, LS 0.2, and a Lookahead/EMA (alpha schedule 0.95^5*(t/T)^3, every 5 steps). Its key addition is data filtering: a small proxy model scores examples and only the highest-loss 512 of every 1024 are used for the main model's update.
findings.relevance: lr 9.0 and wd 0.012 match the CIFAR-100 PR, so it likely started from this file. Hard-example selection is an untested lever. On CIFAR-100 the proxy's cost would fall inside the timed region, and at under 10 epochs the payoff is uncertain.
hypotheses: H5: Hard-example selection via a cheap proxy reduces total time at equal accuracy
H5.1: Proxy-based top-50% loss selection on the airbench96-style net reduces CIFAR-100 time-to-75% despite proxy cost
H8: Lookahead/EMA of weights near the end of training raises final accuracy at a fixed epoch budget

findings.claim: Derandomized alternating horizontal flip beats random flip whenever flipping helps. Its speedup is larger without test-time augmentation (27.1% at 20 epochs without it vs 21.3% with it).
findings.relevance: Test-time augmentation is banned here, so alternating flip should matter more than in the original airbench94 setting.
hypotheses: H7.1: Alternating flip gives a larger accuracy gain in the no-TTA CIFAR-100 setting than random flip, worth at least 0.3 epochs

findings.claim: One-cycle/cyclical LR with a large peak gives super-convergence on CIFAR-10/100 ResNets (e.g. 92.4% in 10k iterations vs 91.2% in 80k with step LR on CIFAR-10). The benefit is larger with limited labeled data.
findings.relevance: Supports a short schedule with a high peak LR and a linear decay to zero (airbench uses a triangular schedule). Tuning schedule shape and length is a cheap lever.
hypotheses: H9: The LR schedule shape (warmup fraction, decay to zero) at a fixed short budget measurably shifts accuracy, so it can trade for epochs
